calc.label: Debt Payoff
calc.metaTitle: Debt Payoff Calculator: Compare Snowball vs Avalanche
calc.metaDescription: Free debt payoff calculator comparing debt snowball and avalanche strategies. Enter balances, APRs, and extra payments to see dates, interest, and payoff order.
calc.introText:
You can clear all three sample debts totaling $19,500 in 34 months and pay $4,783.63 in total interest using the avalanche method, compared to 91 months and $12,291.39 in interest when paying only minimums. 

To decide which debt to pay first, make minimum payments across every balance, send your extra monthly budget to your target debt, and roll each freed minimum payment into the next balance once an account hits zero. The avalanche strategy targets the balance carrying the highest annual percentage rate (APR), while the snowball method targets the smallest balance first to give faster early wins.

This calculator starts preloaded with a store card, a credit card, and a personal loan so you can immediately see the three-plan comparison. Replace the rows with your own balances, interest rates, minimum payments, and extra monthly budget to compare your payoff dates.
calc.howItWorks:
In our internal modeling, we compared avalanche, snowball, and minimum-payment schedules across $19,500 in consumer debt with a $200 extra monthly payment to measure the gap in total interest and completion time. The avalanche strategy clears all three balances in 34 months with $4,783.63 in total interest. The snowball strategy clears the debts in 35 months with $5,120.19 in interest, costing $336.56 more. Paying only minimums stretches the repayment period to 91 months and accumulates $12,291.39 in interest, which is $7,507.76 more interest and 57 additional months compared to avalanche.

The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/blog/how-reduce-your-debt) describes the highest interest rate method as focusing extra payments on your costliest balances to reduce total borrowing costs over the long run. In contrast, the CFPB defines the snowball method as paying off your smallest balance first so you eliminate individual obligations sooner. In our preloaded example, the snowball method eliminates the $2,500 store card in month 10, whereas the avalanche method eliminates its first balance (the $6,000 credit card at 27.99% APR) in month 22. Snowball clears its first debt 12 months sooner than avalanche clears its first, which is a faster early win, and it costs $336.56 in additional interest.

The financial difference between avalanche and snowball depends entirely on your rate spread. When all your debts share the same interest rate, the choice disappears. In our modeling of two debts at an identical 18% APR ($3,000 and $7,000 with a $150 extra payment), both avalanche and snowball finish in exactly 30 months and cost identical interest of $2,464.56. When your smallest balance also happens to carry your highest APR, the two methods follow the exact same payoff order. Modeling a $1,500 balance at 26% APR alongside a $9,000 loan at 9% APR with $100 extra per month produces an identical 35-month timeline, $1,611.43 in total interest, and a month-12 payoff for the first account across both strategies.
calc.howItWorksHeading: Snowball vs Avalanche on Your Numbers

sections.heading: How the Calculator Works
sections.body:
The calculator runs a deterministic month-by-month mathematical simulation to project your payoff dates across all open accounts. Each month, the engine adds interest to every active account by multiplying the current balance by its APR divided by 12. Next, it subtracts the required minimum payment from each account, capping that payment at the remaining balance. Finally, the tool sums your original minimum payments, your extra monthly payment, and any month-one lump sum into a unified monthly budget, directing every unallocated dollar to your target debt before spilling excess funds down the order.

Rolling payments forward is the core mechanism that speeds up both strategies. When you fully pay off an account, that account's required minimum payment does not disappear from your budget. Instead, the engine automatically rolls that freed payment into the extra payment pool for the next debt in line. If a lender sets a minimum payment that falls below the account's monthly accrued interest, the calculator warns you that the balance is not shrinking on that minimum alone. For an individual account payoff or detailed amortization steps, use our [credit card payoff calculator](/credit-card-payoff/) to evaluate single-card minimums.

The model assumes fixed interest rates, on-time payments, no new charges or penalties, and consistent monthly funding throughout the payoff timeline. If you are deciding between paying accounts individually or replacing them with a single personal loan, our [debt consolidation calculator](/debt-consolidation-calculator/) evaluates taking out one new loan rather than ordering payments across existing accounts.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Three Debts and $200 Extra
sections.body:
To see the math in action, examine the baseline scenario preloaded into the calculator. This profile includes three common consumer obligations totaling $19,500 in principal and $515 in base minimum payments. Adding $200 per month raises the total monthly debt budget to $715.

| Debt Name | Starting Balance | APR | Minimum Monthly Payment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Store card | $2,500 | 19.99% | $75 |
| Credit card | $6,000 | 27.99% | $160 |
| Personal loan | $11,000 | 11.00% | $280 |

Here is how the three strategies perform when handling these balances:

| Payoff Strategy | Debt-Free Timeline | Total Interest Paid | Total Amount Paid | Account Payoff Order |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Avalanche | 34 months | $4,783.63 | $24,283.63 | Credit card (mo. 22), Store card (mo. 26), Personal loan (mo. 34) |
| Snowball | 35 months | $5,120.19 | $24,620.19 | Store card (mo. 10), Credit card (mo. 27), Personal loan (mo. 35) |
| Minimums Only | 91 months | $12,291.39 | $31,791.39 | Personal loan (mo. 49), Store card (mo. 50), Credit card (mo. 91) |

Avalanche minimizes total interest charges whenever interest rates differ across accounts, while snowball costs slightly more in exchange for faster early eliminations. With equal interest rates or when your smallest balance also carries your highest rate, the choice between the two methods produces identical costs. This payoff ordering applies to unsecured debts and installment loans that you can prepay without penalty. Our recommendation would change if an account carries a prepayment penalty, if you have access to a 0% promotional rate, or if you hold only a single account.

This multi-debt calculator is not intended for someone carrying only one balance, who should use the credit card payoff calculator instead. It is also not suitable for debts with active 0% promotional periods that should not be prioritized ahead of high-interest accounts.

faqs.question: Which debt should I pay off first?
faqs.answer: Pay off the debt with the highest APR first if you want to pay the least total interest, which is the avalanche method. Choose your smallest balance first if you want faster early wins, which is the snowball method. Regardless of strategy, always make minimum payments on all other accounts.

faqs.question: How long will it take to pay off all my debts?
faqs.answer: Payoff time depends on your total balances, interest rates, and extra payments. In our baseline $19,500 example, paying only minimums takes 91 months. Adding $200 extra per month cuts that timeline to 34 months under avalanche and 35 months under snowball, saving nearly five years of payments.

faqs.question: Does adding a lump sum payment speed up debt payoff?
faqs.answer: Applying a lump sum immediately reduces principal, lowering monthly interest accrual across all remaining months. In our model, adding a $2,000 month-one lump sum to the sample debts reduces avalanche repayment from 34 to 30 months and drops total interest from $4,783.63 to $3,323.03, saving $1,460.60 in interest.

faqs.question: Can I use this calculator for biweekly payments?
faqs.answer: The calculator runs on monthly cycles, but you can approximate biweekly payments by adjusting your extra monthly input. Because 26 biweekly half-payments equal 13 full payments per year, divide your total monthly debt payment by 12 and enter that figure as your extra monthly payment to simulate the extra annual payment.

faqs.question: Can I include a car loan, student loan, or HELOC?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can include any debt that has a fixed balance, an APR, and a monthly minimum payment. Keep in mind that car loans and home equity lines of credit are secured by collateral, and some installment loans carry prepayment penalties that alter the financial advantage of accelerating payoff.

faqs.question: Why might my lender's payoff date differ from this calculator?
faqs.answer: Some lenders add interest daily, while this calculator adds it monthly using APR divided by 12. Differences also occur if your APR is variable, if the lender charges account maintenance fees, or if your actual payment dates vary from month to month.

faqs.question: Can I track debt payoff in Excel or Google Sheets?
faqs.answer: You can replicate this logic in a spreadsheet by creating a row for each month and tracking interest, minimums, extra payments, and rolling balances across columns. This calculator runs those monthly allocation loops automatically, showing instant comparison totals without requiring manual formula maintenance or schedule rebuilding.

faqs.question: Should I pay off debt or invest extra cash?
faqs.answer: Compare your guaranteed debt interest rate against your expected after-tax investment return. Read our guide on whether to [pay off debt or invest](/guides/pay-off-debt-or-invest/) to evaluate your options.

guide3.title: Compound Interest Formula in Excel and Google Sheets
guide3.metaDescription: Calculate compound interest in Excel and Google Sheets. Copy verified FV and mathematical power formulas for lump sums and recurring monthly deposits.
guide3.h1: Compound Interest Formula in Excel and Google Sheets
guide3.cardBlurb: Learn exact formulas to calculate compound interest in Excel and Google Sheets for lump sums and monthly deposits.
guide3.introText:
To calculate compound interest in Excel or Google Sheets, use =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for a lump sum balance or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) when adding regular contributions. Both formulas return the future balance for a fixed interest rate.

The =FV shortcut is accurate only when regular deposits match the compounding frequency, such as monthly additions with monthly compounding.

If you prefer an instant calculation without manually entering spreadsheet syntax, run your figures through our [compound interest calculator](/investing/compound-interest-calculator/) to compare outcomes instantly.

sections.heading: How to Calculate Compound Interest in Excel and Google Sheets
sections.body:
To calculate compound interest in a spreadsheet, enter =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for an initial lump sum or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) for recurring contributions. In these formulas, P represents initial principal, r is the annual interest rate, n is compounding periods per year, and t is total investment years.

In our internal modeling, we ran both formulas on a $10,000 initial balance at a 5% nominal rate over 10 years, confirming that monthly compounding produces an exact future value (FV) of $16,470.09. We verified our mathematical power outputs against a month-by-month calculation loop and checked the built-in function against the documented test case published by [Microsoft Support](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/fv-function), which confirms =FV(0.06/12,10,-200,-500,1) equals $2,581.40.

Spreadsheets require cash outflows to be entered as negative numbers. If you omit the negative signs before regular contributions or initial principal, the formula produces a negative future balance. When regular deposits occur on a different timeline than compounding, such as monthly deposits alongside daily compounding, you must compute an effective periodic rate rather than using a simple rate division.

sections.heading: The Compound Interest Formula Step by Step
sections.body:
The standard compound interest formula evaluates exponential asset growth using the equation A = P*(1 + r/n)^(n*t).

Each component represents a concrete variable in your savings plan:

- A is the final future balance after all interest accrues.
- P is the starting principal balance.
- r is the nominal annual interest rate expressed as a decimal.
- n is the number of times interest compounds per calendar year.
- t is the overall duration of the investment in years.

Consider a starting balance of $10,000 invested at 5% nominal annual interest for 10 years with monthly compounding. In cell format, write =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10). The term 0.05/12 divides the annual percentage rate (APR) into a monthly rate of approximately 0.004167, while 12*10 calculates the 120 total compounding periods. Evaluating this expression yields exactly $16,470.09.

Changing the compounding frequency alters the exponent and periodic divisor. Using the same $10,000 balance at 5% over 10 years, annual compounding (n=1) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/1)^(1*10) produces $16,288.95. Quarterly compounding (n=4) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) yields $16,436.19. Daily compounding (n=365) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/365)^(365*10) grows to $16,486.65. You can also evaluate a lump sum using the built-in future value syntax =FV(0.05/12,12*10,0,-10000), which returns the identical $16,470.09.

sections.heading: Adding Monthly Contributions With FV
sections.body:
When you add recurring savings to an existing investment, use the future value function documented on the [Microsoft Support](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/fv-function) and [Google Docs Editors Help](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093224?hl=en) pages. Both platforms implement the syntax FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]).

The arguments represent specific cash flow parameters:

- rate is the interest rate applied per single period.
- nper is the total count of compounding payment periods.
- pmt is the cash deposit added each period.
- pv is the present value or initial principal balance.
- type indicates payment timing, where 0 represents the end of the period and 1 represents the beginning.

For a $10,000 starting balance with $200 deposited at the end of each month at 5% annual interest for 10 years, enter =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200,-10000). This returns $47,526.55. Over 10 years, your cumulative cash contributions total $34,000, consisting of the $10,000 principal plus $24,000 in monthly additions. Total compound interest earned equals $13,526.55. If you initiate deposits at the beginning of each period instead, enter =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200,-10000,1), which yields $47,655.95.

If you begin with zero initial principal and contribute only regular monthly deposits, omit the principal entry: =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200) yields $31,056.46. When deposits and compounding occur strictly once per year, enter =FV(5%,10,-2400,-10000), returning $46,475.89.

A critical mathematical condition applies: the basic =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) shortcut assumes the contribution schedule matches the compounding frequency. If you contribute $200 monthly while the financial institution compounds interest daily, standard rate division slightly understates growth. To resolve this mismatch, calculate the effective monthly rate using (1+0.05/365)^(365/12)-1, which equals 0.00417507. Entering =FV(0.00417507,12*10,-200,-10000) produces $47,559.87. That creates a $33.32 difference over 10 years compared to the simple monthly division output of $47,526.55.

sections.heading: Daily, Monthly and Yearly Compounding Compared
sections.body:
Increasing the frequency of compounding periods accelerates overall account growth by adding accrued interest to the principal base earlier. To see how deposit institutions handle these daily mechanics, read our review of [how savings account interest is calculated](/guides/how-is-savings-account-interest-calculated/).

The table below models a $10,000 principal deposit earning a 5% nominal annual interest rate over a 10-year term across different compounding frequencies:

| Compounding Frequency | Periodic Divisor (n) | Formula Syntax | Future Value (10 Years) | Effective Annual Percentage Yield (APY) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Annually | 1 | =10000*(1+0.05/1)^(1*10) | $16,288.95 | 5.0000% |
| Quarterly | 4 | =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) | $16,436.19 | 5.0945% |
| Monthly | 12 | =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10) | $16,470.09 | 5.1162% |
| Daily | 365 | =10000*(1+0.05/365)^(365*10) | $16,486.65 | 5.1267% |

Daily compounding produces $197.70 more in accumulated interest than annual compounding on a $10,000 balance over 10 years. For continuous compounding benchmarks, theoretical growth reaches $16,487.21 under identical terms. Annual percentage yield (APY) measures this true annualized return. A 5% nominal annual rate yields an effective 5.1162% under monthly compounding and 5.1267% under daily compounding.

sections.heading: Common Spreadsheet Mistakes
sections.body:
Formulas fail when users mismatch timing inputs or violate spreadsheet sign rules. Avoid these three common calculation errors:

1. Entering annual interest rates against monthly periods. Passing an unadjusted annual rate such as 5% or 0.05 alongside 120 monthly periods in =FV(0.05, 120, -200, -10000) causes the software to apply a 5% return each individual month. This mistake inflates the projected balance to $4,880,767.80 instead of the true $47,526.55 balance. Always divide the annual rate by your annual periods.
2. Omitting negative signs on outgoing deposits and principal. Microsoft Support documents the sign convention for these functions. Money deposited represents cash leaving your hand, which must be entered as a negative number. Writing =FV(0.05/12, 120, 200, 10000) yields -$47,526.55. Insert negative signs before payment and present value arguments to display positive savings balances.
3. Ignoring compounding and contribution schedule mismatches. The standard FV formula assumes periodic contributions occur on the identical schedule as interest compounding. If you deposit funds monthly but earn interest compounded daily, using naive monthly division understates growth. Converting your nominal daily rate into an effective monthly rate eliminates this variance.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
To model investment compounding accurately, use =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) whenever your deposit frequency matches your compounding schedule, or =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for fixed lump-sum balances. 

This spreadsheet modeling approach is not suitable for individuals seeking instant figures without formula entry, nor does it accommodate variable-rate products. Readers requiring fast comparisons across custom scenarios can model their numbers using our [compound interest calculator](/investing/compound-interest-calculator/).

Our recommendation would change if deposit accounts adjust to floating rates, if tax withholding or custodial platform fees are subtracted from annual growth, or if a spreadsheet platform updates its foundational financial argument conventions. For your next step, copy our verified formulas into your personal workbook to audit your current wealth accumulation schedule.

faqs.question: How to calculate compound interest in Excel?
faqs.answer: Calculate compound interest in Excel using =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for a lump sum or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -pmt, -pv) for recurring payments. For example, a $10,000 lump sum at 5% interest for 10 years compounded monthly is entered as =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10), which outputs $16,470.09. Enter outgoing investments as negative numbers to ensure the function outputs a positive balance.

faqs.question: Is compound interest calculated monthly or yearly?
faqs.answer: Compound interest can compound on any schedule specified by the financial institution, commonly daily, monthly, or yearly. On a $10,000 balance at 5% over 10 years, annual compounding produces $16,288.95 while monthly compounding produces $16,470.09.

faqs.question: Does the same compound interest formula work in Google Sheets?
faqs.answer: Yes, Google Sheets uses the exact same syntax and argument order as Excel for calculating compound interest. Both applications accept the standard mathematical power equation =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) as well as the built-in financial function =FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]).

faqs.question: How do you calculate quarterly or half-yearly compounding?
faqs.answer: Calculate quarterly compounding by setting the periodic divisor n to 4, and half-yearly compounding by setting n to 2. For a $10,000 investment at 5% for 10 years compounded quarterly, the formula =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) produces exactly $16,436.19. To model semi-annual compounding under the same parameters, replace the divisor and multiplier with 2 in the formula =P*(1+r/2)^(2*t).

faqs.question: How do you include monthly deposits in the compound interest formula?
faqs.answer: Include monthly deposits by using the future value function =FV(rate/12, 12*years, -monthly_deposit, -initial_principal). For a $10,000 starting balance with $200 added at the end of each month at 5% interest over 10 years, enter =FV(0.05/12, 12*10, -200, -10000). This returns $47,526.55, reflecting $34,000 in total out-of-pocket deposits and $13,526.55 in earned compound interest.

faqs.question: What interest rate should you enter in spreadsheet formulas?
faqs.answer: Enter the periodic interest rate, which is the nominal annual rate divided by the number of compounding periods per year. If your annual rate is 5% and interest compounds monthly, enter 0.05/12 or 5%/12 as the rate argument. Entering the full annual rate of 0.05 alongside 120 monthly periods erroneously calculates 5% growth per month, severely overstating results.

guide3.disclaimerText: This guide provides general educational information about spreadsheet formulas and financial calculations, not personalized investment or financial advice.

guide4.title: Property Tax by State: What It Adds to Your Mortgage Payment
guide4.metaDescription: See what property taxes add to a monthly mortgage payment by state, from $97 in Hawaii to $627 in New Jersey on a $400,000 home.
guide4.h1: Property Tax by State: What It Adds to Your Mortgage Payment
guide4.cardBlurb: Compare monthly property tax costs across all 50 states on a $400,000 home and see how escrow charges alter your housing budget.
guide4.introText:
Property tax adds roughly (effective rate x home price) / 12 to your monthly principal and interest payment, ranging from about $97 a month in Hawaii to about $627 a month in New Jersey and Illinois on a $400,000 home. 

Evaluating the tax baseline in your target region helps protect against unexpected escrow shortages after closing. The breakdown below details the monthly property tax impact across all 50 states using standardized baseline pricing.

sections.heading: Property Tax Added to a $400,000 Mortgage by State
sections.body:
Property tax adds about (effective rate x home price) / 12 a month to a borrower's housing expense, which translates to about $97 in Hawaii up to about $627 in New Jersey and Illinois on a $400,000 home.

The District of Columbia carries an effective property tax rate of 0.60%, which adds $200 a month on a $400,000 residence and sits outside the 50-state ranking. Across the entire country, the median state effective rate results in a monthly property tax charge of about $263.

sections.heading: How the Estimate Works
sections.body:
To calculate the monthly tax portion of a mortgage payment, multiply your home purchase price by the state effective rate and divide the total by 12.

In our internal modeling, we converted each state's effective rate to a monthly dollar figure on a $400,000 home using baseline data from the [Tax Foundation](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/property-taxes-by-state-county/). The underlying data comes from the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) of the U.S. Census Bureau. An effective property tax rate represents the percentage of total owner-occupied market value paid in taxes.

State averages often conceal dramatic county-level variations. In New Jersey, for example, county-level effective rates span from 0.93% in Cape May County to 2.47% in Camden County. That means an identical $400,000 purchase incurs about $310 a month in property taxes in Cape May County, but about $823 a month in Camden County. A buyer relying solely on the New Jersey state average of $627 a month faces a substantial discrepancy when closing on a home in either jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Highest and Lowest Property Tax States
sections.body:
The five states with the highest monthly property taxes on a $400,000 home are New Jersey ($627), Illinois ($627), Connecticut ($513), Vermont ($503), and New Hampshire ($500).

A higher monthly tax leaves less of your budget for the loan payment. You can test how a higher or lower tax changes what you can afford with our [mortgage affordability calculator](/mortgage/affordability-calculator/).

Conversely, the five lowest property tax states for owner-occupied housing are Hawaii ($97 at 0.29%), Alabama ($123 at 0.37%), Utah ($160 at 0.48%), Arizona ($160 at 0.48%), and South Carolina ($163 at 0.49%).

sections.heading: What Else Goes Into Escrow
sections.body:
Property tax is only one piece of a mortgage payment.

Our state comparison table models property taxes alone, meaning homeowners insurance premiums and private mortgage insurance remain excluded from these specific figures. Homeowners association (HOA) dues are also not included. To calculate your comprehensive monthly housing obligation including all loan and insurance components, utilize our [PITI mortgage calculator](/mortgage/piti-calculator/), where PITI stands for principal, interest, taxes, and insurance.

If you know your county's effective rate, use it in the same formula instead of the state figure. Our guide to [mortgage mistakes before applying](/guides/mortgage-mistakes-before-applying/) covers other costs buyers overlook.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
Property tax can add from about $97 to about $627 a month on a $400,000 home depending on state, and your county rate decides the real number.

This benchmark modeling applies to owner-occupied residential properties assessed at the exact $400,000 baseline price. This analysis is not applicable to residential tenants, who pay shelter expenses via lease agreements rather than direct tax bills, nor does it capture multi-million-dollar purchases without linear adjustment. If your home purchase differs from $400,000, scale the monthly dollar figures proportionally by multiplying the state rate against your target valuation before dividing by 12.

Our conclusions would change if local taxing jurisdictions revise their assessment ratios, if state legislatures expand homestead exemption limits, or if the Tax Foundation publishes updated effective rates. Multiply your own price by your county's effective rate and divide by 12 before you make an offer.

faqs.question: Does a mortgage calculator include property tax and insurance?
faqs.answer: Some mortgage calculators cover only principal and interest, while others add property tax and insurance. To compute your complete monthly housing expense including tax and insurance escrows, enter your loan and property details into our [PITI mortgage calculator](/mortgage/piti-calculator/).

faqs.question: How much is property tax on a $400,000 house in the highest and lowest states?
faqs.answer: On a $400,000 home, property taxes add about $627 a month in New Jersey and Illinois at the top of the state rankings, compared to about $97 a month in Hawaii at the bottom. The median state level sits at roughly $263 a month.

faqs.question: What is an effective property tax rate?
faqs.answer: An effective property tax rate measures the annual property tax paid as a percentage of the total market value of owner-occupied housing. It lets you compare states on one scale.

faqs.question: Why do property taxes differ inside the same state?
faqs.answer: Rates differ by county inside a state. For instance, New Jersey county rates span from 0.93% in Cape May County to 2.47% in Camden County, creating very different monthly payments on identical home prices.

faqs.question: Is homeowners insurance included in the monthly property tax figures?
faqs.answer: Homeowners insurance is not included in the monthly property tax figures on this page.

faqs.question: How do I calculate monthly property taxes for my specific home price?
faqs.answer: To calculate monthly property taxes for your specific home price, multiply your target purchase price by your local effective tax rate percentage and divide the resulting figure by 12.

Reviewing the spread between your highest and lowest borrowing rates clarifies whether the interest savings justify delaying that first account closure.
